To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the devotional voice of early modern England was not gendered; that the discursive horizons of devotional texts were not gendered; and that the discursive horizon of the genre of spiritual memoirs was gendered (Narvesons, 134).

(a) gender is not a significant marker for the devotional voice, (b) the devotional voice is not a significant indicator of gender, (c) the discursive horizon for devotional writing is the Bible, and (d) gender is a significant marker for devotional writing that is not about the Bible.
the devotional voice is a rhetorical construct that suppresses gender, and that the devotional mode tends to suppress gender as well.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the ways in which early modern readers and writers of religious texts, in their own writings, constructed and negotiated their own identities in the context of a culture in which the authority and power of the printed word was increasingly being recognized. In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Narveson's work offers a new perspective on the emergence of identity in early modern writing, and that it does so with a thorough and balanced examination of gender.
the Reformation period is one of transition in the development of identity through authorial voice.

the Reformation was not the end of a medieval world view but rather a new beginning, and that the process of reading and writing was a central part of the process of identity formation in this new world, and that gender was not as important as other factors, such as genre, class, and education in the formation of identity through reading and writing practices in this period.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the "discursive horizontals" of a particular genre, or even of a specific text, can be a powerful tool for shaping the voice of a reader/writer, and for the reader to shape a response.
genre and gender are two of the discursive horizons that writers and readers use to construct their identities in the process of reading and writing, but they are not the only two.
genre and gender are not the same, and that they are not mutually exclusive, either.
The main takeaway from our work is that
genre is a key element in identity formation. …
the Reformation's emphasis on the reader's experience of the text as a means to a spiritual end is a powerful force in the construction of identity, whether the reader is male or female.

the voice in a text is always a constructed one, a rhetorical one; and that it is always a voice that speaks to an implied reader, and is therefore always in dialogue, whether with a real or imagined audience.
